Normative cross-language conformance vectors for apple-purchase-receipt-verifier.
One case per semantic fact: java/, node/, python/, swift/, go/, ruby/, rust/, php/ and dotnet/
each assert many of these under their own test names, and the duplicates are merged here.
Every expectation in this file was derived by hand from the four test-suite inventories,
from PLAN.md sections 2.1-2.3, from COMPARISON.md and from the fixture generator
(java/src/test/.../FixtureGeneratorTest.java) plus fixtures/generated/manifest.json.
NOTHING here was produced by running an implementation and recording what it did:
a vector that disagrees with an implementation is a bug report against that implementation
until a human decides otherwise.

Paths in "fields" are language-neutral. Scalars use the shared API names from PLAN.md section 3
(camelCase) for verifyTransaction/verifyAppTransaction/verifyRaw/verifyReceipt, and the literal
Apple wire keys (snake_case) for verifyReceiptEndpoint. "x.length" is a collection size.
"list[key=value].field" selects the single element of list whose key equals value.
"unknownAttributes[9999][0]" indexes the raw values recorded for receipt attribute type 9999,
expressed as a lowercase hex string. Dates are ISO-8601 UTC strings; claims that Apple ships as
epoch milliseconds (signedDate, receiptCreationDate) stay numbers. null means "absent or unset".
A field a case does not list is simply not pinned by that case.

Certificate-validity windows are judged at the payload signedDate / receipt creationDate, and
where the input states neither (for a receipt: a creation date that is missing, empty,
unreadable or stated twice, or a top-level attribute entry that cannot be read), at the SYSTEM clock — never at an injected one (PLAN.md 2.1
step 4, 2.2 step 2). The expired-chain cases are therefore deterministic. "clock" appears where
the answer genuinely moves with time — the max-signed-age staleness rule and the request_date
triple of the verifyReceipt endpoint — and, on the four dateless inputs, precisely to pin that
the answer does NOT move: a receipt or payload carrying no date of its own, verified under a
clock planted inside an expired certificate's window or far past a live one's, must reach the
verdict it reaches on real time. A caller injecting a clock to test staleness, or to work
around clock skew, must not thereby accept a chain that is expired. verifyReceipt cases cannot
carry a clock at all — the schema refuses one — because ReceiptVerifier takes no clock
parameter in any port. Where the schema does allow one, a runner MUST hand the case's clock to
the verifier rather than fake time; a case carrying a clock that is run against the system
clock is not running the case.

Every fixture records the SHA-256 of its DECODED logical bytes (post-codec: the file bytes for
raw, the base64-decoded bytes for base64, the trimmed UTF-8 for utf8). contentSha256 is not
documentation: tools/lint-cases.mjs re-hashes every registered fixture, and so does every
adapter — over the whole registry before any case runs, and again for each fixture a case
loads. A fixture that is regenerated, re-encoded or quietly edited fails loudly in every
language instead of silently changing what these vectors mean.

Four places where the ports had drifted apart were adjudicated and are pinned here: the
certificate-validity fallback clock (the dateless cases), the typed endpoint environment
(config.environment is the enum, and both values are exercised), and a receipt attribute type
above 2^31-1, which every port must reject as INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT rather than rename or
clamp. The fourth — verifyReceiptCore being public in every port, so no endpoint has to build a
wildcard-bundle-id verifier to reach it — changes no observable answer, so no vector can hold
it; the native suites carry that one.

"fault" names the one intentional defect of a negative case. It is documentation, not an
assertion: implementations are not required to report it, only to report the given reason.

Receipt base64 (added 2026-09-04, rule replaced 2026-09-23). Every runner decodes a base64 fixture itself and hands DER to the library, so no verifyReceipt case can say how a port treats the string a client actually sent. The text codec and the verifyReceiptBase64 operation close that: the fixture bytes go to the string entry point verbatim, and a verifyReceiptEndpoint case over a text fixture puts them in receipt-data verbatim. The rule they pin is the one Apple's verifyReceipt applies, measured on 2026-09-23 against the production and sandbox endpoints with genuine receipts (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md): receipt-data is accepted if and only if it is non-empty standard-alphabet base64 ([A-Za-z0-9+/]) carrying exactly the canonical '=' padding for its data length, and nothing else. Whitespace anywhere (a trailing line feed, line breaks at 64 or 76 columns, a leading space), the base64url alphabet, omitted, partial or extra padding, anything after the padding, an impossible length and the empty string are all INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT (21002 at the endpoint). Unused low bits in the last data character are accepted, because Apple accepts them. The rule this replaced accepted everything Foundation's base64EncodedString(options:) can emit, base64url, omitted padding and line breaks included; it was reasoned from the documentation and never measured, and Apple refuses all of those, so seven accept-* cases became reject-*.

Hostile JWS (added 2026-09-05). Six inputs that Python's coverage-guided fuzzing walked out of the library as bare exceptions rather than verdicts are pinned here, so that all nine ports answer them and answer them the same way. A seventh input sits with them carrying no defect at all: the same signedDate spelled 1722945600000.0, which must verify, because a port could otherwise pass the out-of-range vector by refusing every number that is not a bare integer. Each is a real JWS over the generated test PKI carrying exactly one mutation; the header is signed in its hostile state so the ES256 signature covers the bytes served, and a mutated certificate is re-signed by its issuer so a broken issuer signature can never be the first thing a port objects to. The reasons were adjudicated against Node and Python, which already agreed on three of the five, and on the fourth the majority was overruled for the reason that case states: x5c entries that are not strings are INVALID_JWS_FORMAT, a signedDate of 1e300 is INVALID_CHAIN, a certificate that stops decoding inside its extension block is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, an unimplemented EC curve on the intermediate is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, and a certificate claiming X.509 version 11 is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, and a certificate carrying the same extension twice is INVALID_CERTIFICATE. The per-case descriptions carry the reasoning for each. What these five have in common is where the defect sits: in the JWS header and in the x5c certificates, both of which every port decodes BEFORE the signature that would have rejected them, and neither of which any signature in the input authenticates. An eighth input joined them when the x5c[2] differential was closed: the third x5c entry holding base64 of "not a certificate", which java alone rejected because java alone parsed that entry. The other eight ports verified the JWS, and the majority lost to the same rule the unimplemented curve lost to — pinning acceptance would have made java drop a rejection it already makes. Every port now parses all three entries; none of them trusts the third, which is what the differential was always about.

Receipt signer certificates (added 2026-09-05). The four certificate mutations above sit in a JWS header, and four ports answered them from checks written on the JWS path alone (node, python, ruby and dotnet; rust and php had them in a shared certificate parser, and java, swift and go get them from a platform decoder). So the same four mutations — X.509 version 11, a duplicated basicConstraints, an unassigned EC curve and an extension block that stops decoding — are built into the certificate a legacy PKCS#7 receipt is signed by, and carry the reason their JWS twins carry: INVALID_CERTIFICATE. Each receipt is genuine in every other respect, with the signer re-signed by the intermediate wherever the mutation touched its TBS, so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. The curve case is the one where the signer's KEY is the mutation: the receipt is signed with a real P-256 key whose certificate then names a curve that does not exist, so the port has to refuse the certificate before it can reach the signature — and it must not answer instead that the key is not RSA, which is a different input.

Compact-JWS segments that are empty or are not JSON objects (added 2026-09-05). RFC 7515 7.1 gives a compact JWS three base64url segments whose first two decode to JSON OBJECTS, and nothing here said what happens when one is empty or decodes to an array or a bare scalar. Six inputs pin it, all INVALID_JWS_FORMAT: the whole input `..`, an empty header, an empty payload, a header that is a JSON array, a header that is a bare scalar, and a payload that is a JSON array. The two with the defect in the PAYLOAD carry a genuine header and signature, so a port answers about the payload rather than about the certificates in a fake header; the four with the defect in the header need no signing, because the header is read first. Two things make these worth pinning rather than assuming. An empty segment is valid base64url of zero bytes, and a JSON reader that answers "nothing" instead of raising hands the caller a null the next line dereferences — which is how `..` left java as a NullPointerException rather than a verdict. And an empty or non-object PAYLOAD makes every claim read as absent, which fails OPEN: a payload stating no signedDate moves certificate validity onto the current-time fallback and silences the staleness rule, the same pair transaction/reject-signed-date-out-of-range guards from the other side.

Resource bounds (added 2026-09-05, rewritten 2026-09-23). The byte limits are a contract, and they are Apple's. Measured on 2026-09-23 against both https://buy.itunes.apple.com/verifyReceipt and the sandbox endpoint: a request body of 3,145,728 bytes is answered normally and one of 3,145,729 bytes gets HTTP 413, and the limit counts UTF-8 bytes, not characters: 3,145,729 bytes of U+00E9 (only 1,572,874 characters) also got 413, while 3,145,727 bytes of it got 200. So every port applies exactly these limits, as fixed constants no caller can change. A raw request body over 3,145,728 UTF-8 bytes is status 21002 with the result-only reason REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, decided before the body is parsed; a caller's HTTP layer can map it to 413 as Apple does. A receipt over 3,145,728 bytes, measured on the base64 string before it is decoded and again on the DER, is INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT (21002 at the endpoint). A request body nesting more than 64 arrays and objects at once is 21002 with MALFORMED_REQUEST. A compact JWS over 262,144 bytes is INVALID_JWS_FORMAT. At or under each limit nothing may be refused for its size. The resource-bounds vectors hold each number from both sides where an input can say so. Their inputs are real files under fixtures/limits/, registered like every other fixture, so every runner reads identical bytes; tools/generate-limit-fixtures.mjs wrote them and says how each is built, and git stores their padding compressed to a few kilobytes. None contains a lone surrogate, so ports need not agree on how one would be counted. A verifyReceiptEndpoint case may name its input as requestBody instead of fixture: that text fixture is the WHOLE raw request body, handed to the port's raw-body entry point (the one that parses JSON) rather than wrapped as receipt-data by the runner. expected.failureReason on an endpoint case pins the reason the result carries, beside the wire fields because it is not on the wire: any thrown reason, or one of the result-only MALFORMED_REQUEST, REQUEST_TOO_LARGE and INTERNAL_ERROR, which no verifier ever throws. The ASN.1 node budgets stay port-local (200,000 nodes per parse in ruby, 100,000 in rust and go, 20,000 in php, none elsewhere), so for nodes the contract states the floor beneath them: every port MUST accept a well-formed, correctly signed receipt whose largest single ASN.1 parse holds up to 20,000 nodes. A node is one TLV, counted descending into constructed values only, because a primitive OCTET STRING's contents (an in-app purchase, an attribute value, the encapsulated payload) are a separate parse with a separate budget in every port that has one. Two receipts pin the accepting side, one number each: `receipt-byte-floor` is 1,034,681 bytes at 9,237 nodes and `receipt-node-floor` is 19,897 nodes at 74,569 bytes. One receipt under both limits would not do it: a port could lower either limit to just above what that single receipt happened to use, which is what the 809,069-byte, 16,037-node receipt they replace allowed. The byte-floor receipt, 1,379,576 characters of base64, now also runs through verifyReceiptEndpoint. The DER cap is held from both sides by genuine receipts in the byte-floor shape: `receipt-at-der-cap` is a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of exactly 3,145,728 bytes that every port MUST accept, and `receipt-over-der-cap` is the same receipt one product-id character longer, 3,145,729 bytes, well-formed and correctly signed, so the cap is the only thing that can refuse it. Both carry 9,237 nodes. They run through verifyReceipt only: the base64 cap is 3,145,728 characters, which decode to at most 2,359,296 bytes of DER, so a DER receipt at the cap is reachable only through the raw-DER entry point and never through verifyReceiptBase64 or the endpoint. The string side of the receipt cap is held from below by `limit-receipt-b64-at-cap`, the canonical base64 of a genuinely signed receipt of exactly 2,359,296 bytes, which is 3,145,728 characters: canonical base64 admits nothing around it, so no padding can stretch a smaller receipt to the cap.

Legacy receipt ids (added 2026-09-21). Four attribute types the library used to leave raw in unknownAttributes are modelled: app-level 1 (app item id), 15 (download id) and 16 (version external identifier), and in-app 1713 (is trial period). None is on Apple's archived Receipt Fields chapter. They were established by decoding a genuine production receipt and lining its attributes up against the answer Apple's verifyReceipt endpoint gives for the same receipt, and against Apple's published response reference. All four are INTEGER attributes, decoded like 1711. At the endpoint, attribute 1 is echoed under BOTH adam_id and app_item_id — Apple's reference defines adam_id as "See app_item_id" — and the three app-level ids are JSON numbers while 1713 is the string "true"/"false", exactly like 1719. An attribute a receipt does not carry leaves its key OUT of the answer rather than emitting JSON null, and a value of 0 is a value: Apple's sandbox sends 0 for the three ids. The fixture's download id is 2^53+1, the first integer an IEEE-754 double cannot hold, because Apple's real download_id values run to eighteen digits: a port carrying receipt integers as a JavaScript number answers 9007199254740992 here, or refuses the receipt, and either way the vector catches it.

Prior-art vectors (added 2026-09-22). Seven cases from the audit of the tikhop/TPInAppReceipt test suite and the objc.io "Receipt Validation" walkthrough recorded in PLAN.md's prior-art table. Two of them pin the device hash against Apple-signed bytes rather than against bytes this repository generated: TPInAppReceipt's HashVerifierTests publishes the device identifier of the genuine sandbox receipt vendored under fixtures/public-receipts/, and SHA1(deviceId bytes || attribute 4 || the DER of attribute 2) over it reproduces that receipt's attribute 5 byte for byte, so a port whose concatenation order, UUID byte order or bundle-id encoding is wrong cannot pass by agreeing with the generator that made the fixture. One pins that attribute 2 is compared byte for byte, so a bundle id differing only in the case of one letter is WRONG_BUNDLE_ID. Four are receipts whose single defect sits in the CMS structure rather than in a certificate or in the payload, all from the generator java/src/test/.../ReceiptCmsDefectFixtures.java: a receipt-signing end entity standing where the intermediate belongs, with the signer genuinely issued by it and basicConstraints the only objection (INVALID_CHAIN); the intermediate simply absent from the bag (INVALID_CHAIN, the other way an issuer can be wrong); a SignerInfo signature of zero bytes, which is well-formed DER, so a port must reach verification and take a negative answer from it (INVALID_SIGNATURE); and a CMS signed over zero bytes of encapsulated content, so the chain, the purpose and the signature are all genuine and the empty payload is the only thing left to object to (INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT). The audit also asked for receiptType assertions on the genuine receipts. receipt/verify-genuine-sandbox-g5-against-apple-roots already pins "ProductionSandbox" on genuine Apple bytes, and nothing here can pin "Production" on them: both genuine receipts in the corpus are sandbox receipts, which fixtures/public-receipts/README.md records as the cost of removing the production one, so the generated receipt-type-production fixture carries that value instead.

x5c spelling (added 2026-09-23). RFC 7515 section 4.1.6 makes every x5c entry base64 of a DER certificate: the standard alphabet of RFC 4648 section 4, not base64url, and nothing in RFC 7515 lets an entry carry whitespace. So a character outside that alphabet, a base64url '-' or '_', and a line break are each INVALID_CERTIFICATE, never skipped or translated on the way to a genuine certificate. Three vectors pin it on x5c[0], each signed in its mutated state so the spelling is the only defect: before them, six ports skipped a junk character, four read the base64url alphabet and eight stripped line breaks, and each of those VERIFIED the JWS. Padding joined the family the same day: an entry with its '=' omitted, or with one '=' more than its length calls for, is INVALID_CERTIFICATE too, so an x5c entry now follows the receipt-data rule exactly (standard alphabet, canonical padding, nothing else) and a violation is reported as a certificate defect.

Base64 spellings (added 2026-09-23). The decodeBase64 cases are the one list of base64 spellings every port runs, replacing the nine per-port lists that had drifted apart. Each case is a group: every string in input.texts must get the same answer, and the runner checks each string on its own and names the case id, the index and the escaped string when one fails. An ok group pins expected.bytesHex, the exact bytes every string decodes to; an error group is refused. "decoders" names the decoders a group runs through, each called directly rather than through a verifier: "receipt-data" is the port's receipt-data decoder, and a refusal from it is INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT; "x5c" is the port's x5c-entry decoder, and a refusal from it is INVALID_CERTIFICATE. Error groups state INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT, the receipt-data answer, and a runner maps it to INVALID_CERTIFICATE for x5c; that mapping lives here and in the schema, never per case. The rule is the one the Receipt base64 and x5c spelling paragraphs above state: non-empty standard-alphabet base64 with exactly the canonical '=' padding and nothing else, unused low bits of the last data character accepted, as Apple's verifyReceipt answered on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md). The list is the union of every spelling the ports' own decoder tests, x5c spelling tests and endpoint tests used, with exact duplicates dropped, extended to every row of the evidence table at the three padding lengths, every value of the unused trailing bits, every ASCII whitespace character and the alphabet's range boundaries. tools/lint-cases.mjs re-derives each answer from the rule and refuses a string listed twice. One spelling cannot live here because JSON text cannot hold it: a string that is not valid UTF-8 (ruby's "QU\xffD".b), which stays in the ruby suite.

cases.description: The shared generated StoreKit 2 transaction JWS verifies against its own pinned root and decodes to the manifested claims.
A transaction whose bundleId claim is not the configured one is rejected on the claim check, after the signature and chain pass.
A Sandbox transaction offered to a Production-only accept set is rejected (PLAN.md D3: environment routing is an accept-set).
The generated test chain must not verify against the real pinned Apple JWS roots — anchor pinning, not system trust.

With a max signed age configured, a payload signed longer ago than that is rejected as stale — here months before the pinned verification time. The staleness rule is the only verdict in this file that moves with the clock.

The same payload and the same 60-second max age as the stale case, verified 60 seconds after its signedDate: an age exactly equal to the maximum is still fresh. Pins the rule as "older than the maximum", not "at least as old as".

One second later the same payload under the same configuration is stale. This case and the one above differ in nothing but the injected clock, so together they pin the exact boundary of the max-signed-age rule and prove the clock is what decides it.

A clock an hour before the signedDate leaves the payload fresh: age runs from the signing time to now, and a payload from the future is not stale. Catches an implementation that compares the magnitude of the difference instead of its sign.

A JWS leaf lacking marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped alongside the fixture (PLAN.md 2.1 step 3). Not exercised by the Java suite today, which asserts the same fact against a run-time generated PKI instead.
A JWS intermediate lacking WWDR marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1 is rejected against its own pinned root. Not exercised by the Java suite today.
Chain validity is judged at the payload signedDate, not at verification time: a 2020-06-01 payload signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4).

The same expired chain signing a 2024-08-06 payload is rejected: the signedDate falls outside the certificate validity window. Deterministic — the window is fixed and already in the past, so no clock is needed.
Apple's own app-store-server-library mock transactionInfo verifies against Apple's vendored test CA — cross-library parity on the exact upstream bytes.
Apple's wrongBundleId mock fixture is rejected on the bundle-id claim check.
Apple's missingX5CHeaderClaim mock fixture is rejected at header parsing: no x5c means no chain to validate (PLAN.md 2.1 step 2).
An Xcode/StoreKit-Test signed transaction carries a single self-signed certificate in x5c; requiring exactly three certificates rejects it before any chain work.
The shared generated Sandbox AppTransaction verifies and decodes to the manifested claims; a Sandbox receiptType needs no appAppleId binding.
An AppTransaction carries no signedDate, so its age is measured from receiptCreationDate (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4). Thirty seconds after that date, under a 60-second max age, it is fresh.
Sixty-one seconds after the same receiptCreationDate the AppTransaction is stale. An implementation that only ever ages a payload by signedDate would find no anchor here and accept it.

A Production AppTransaction whose appAppleId claim matches the configured one verifies. Not exercised by the Java suite against this fixture; Java asserts the same fact against a run-time generated PKI.
In Production the appAppleId claim is binding: a mismatch is rejected (PLAN.md 2.1 step 6).
verifyRaw validates chain and signature but enforces no claim: a verifier configured for a different bundle id still returns the decoded claims unchanged.
Apple's mock renewalInfo has no bundleId claim, so it is only reachable through verifyRaw; chain and signature still hold against Apple's test CA.
Apple's mock App Store Server Notification V2 payload verifies through verifyRaw against Apple's test CA.
The shared generated PKCS#7 receipt verifies, its SHA-1 device hash matches the supplied GUID, and every modelled attribute decodes to the manifested value.
Device binding is enforced when a GUID is supplied: flipping the low bit of the first GUID byte breaks SHA1(guid || opaque || bundleIdBytes) against attribute 5.
A receipt issued for another app is rejected on the bundle-id check, after chain, signer purpose and signature pass.
A byte-identical payload signed by a second, independently generated receipt PKI is rejected against the first PKI root.
Xcode-style receipts wrap the attribute SET in an extra OCTET STRING; parsers must unwrap it rather than reject the receipt.

A signer leaf lacking OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped with the fixture (PLAN.md D13 — closes the developer-certificate forgery hole).
Receipt chain validity is judged at the receipt creation date (attribute 12): a 2020-06-01 receipt signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.2 step 2).
The same expired receipt chain signing a 2024-08-06 receipt is rejected: the creation date falls outside the certificate validity window. Deterministic — the window is fixed and already in the past.
Attribute types the library does not model are surfaced raw rather than dropped (PLAN.md D10): the shared receipt carries type 9999 with value bytes 01 02 03.
A genuine Apple-signed sandbox receipt on the newer G5 signing chain verifies against the real pinned Apple receipt roots.
A genuine legacy receipt with a full SHA-1 signing chain and 187 in-app purchases verifies against the real pinned Apple receipt roots.

An Xcode-signed receipt carrying real purchases must not verify against the real Apple roots. The configured bundle id is the literal placeholder "*": the chain fails long before any bundle-id comparison.

A genuine Xcode-generated app receipt from Apple's own test data is rejected against the real Apple roots. Chain validation runs before the signer-purpose check, so the reason is INVALID_CHAIN and not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (PLAN.md 2.2 step 3).

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint answers status 0 for a sandbox receipt on a sandbox instance, rendering numbers as strings and dates as Apple's three-field triple. This case pins no clock, so request_date* is whatever the system clock says and is left unasserted; endpoint/request-date-is-the-verification-clock pins it instead.

request_date is the instant the endpoint answered, so the clock drives it — and drives nothing else: the receipt's own creation date is read from the signed bytes and does not move. The three renderings are Apple's triple: Etc/GMT text, epoch milliseconds as a string, and the same instant in America/Los_Angeles.
A sandbox receipt presented to a production instance routes to 21007 and the response carries neither receipt nor environment.
A receipt that does not chain to the endpoint trust anchors answers 21003 (could not be authenticated), never 21002.
receipt_type "Production" on a production instance answers 0.
receipt_type "Production" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" counts as production (PLAN.md D10 fail-closed routing set).
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" is a sandbox type despite the prefix; on a production instance it answers 21007. The misroute this case pins was found by adversarial review.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" on a sandbox instance answers 0.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox (fail closed), so a production instance answers 21007.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox and answers 0 there.

A receipt attribute whose type INTEGER is 2^31, one past the largest signed 32-bit value. The receipt is sound in every other way: trusted chain, valid CMS signature, correct device hash, real bundle id. Because the step-2 walk cannot read that entry's type, the creation date is not used and the chain is judged at the system clock; it is valid then, the signature verifies, and the full payload parse (step 5) refuses the type. A trusted signer signed content the library cannot represent, which is INTERNAL_ERROR, not a malformed client request. Failing closed is still the decision: mapping an unrepresentable type onto a sentinel such as -1, or filing it under unknownAttributes under a renamed key, makes two ports disagree about what the same bytes contain. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

The same over-range attribute type reaches the endpoint as 21009 (INTERNAL_ERROR), not 21002 and not 21003: the receipt authenticates, and it is signed content the library cannot represent. 21002 would tell an app server the client sent a malformed receipt and invite it to deny a paying user. Pins the reason mapping as well as the rejection. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

A receipt carrying no attribute 12 verifies: the creation date is optional, and with none to anchor on, certificate validity is judged at the system clock (PLAN.md 2.2 step 2). The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050. The companion endpoint cases pin the other half — that "current time" here means the system clock, not an injectable one.

The dateless receipt under a chain that expired in 2021, answered with the clock pinned to 2020-06-01 — inside that chain's validity window. It stays 21003. An injected clock reaches the request_date triple and the max-signed-age rule, never a certificate-validity instant: a caller who injects a clock to test staleness, or to paper over clock skew, must not thereby accept an expired chain. A port that routed the "else current time" fallback through its clock answers 0 here.

The other direction, on a chain valid until 2050: the same dateless receipt answered with the clock pinned to 2099 is still 0. The clock stamps request_date and nothing else, so it can neither authenticate an expired chain nor expire a live one. receipt_creation_date is absent from the body because the receipt states none — the endpoint does not substitute "now" for it.

The JWS half of the same rule. A payload carrying neither signedDate nor receiptCreationDate, signed by a chain that expired in 2021, verified with the clock pinned to 2020-06-01 — inside that window — and a max signed age configured, so the clock does have a legitimate consumer here. It is still INVALID_CHAIN: the staleness rule may read the injected clock, the certificate-validity fallback may not.

A payload that states no signing time cannot be measured against a maximum age, so the max-signed-age rule does not apply: 60 seconds configured and the clock pinned to 2099, and it still verifies. Measuring the clock against itself — treating "now" as the signing time — would make every such payload eternally fresh by accident rather than by rule, and routing the certificate-validity fallback through the same clock would instead make this INVALID_CHAIN, since the chain expires in 2050.

One character of the payload segment was rewritten after the JWS was signed, so the ES256 signature no longer covers the bytes served. Everything a port checks before the signature is deliberately intact: the header is the original one, its three x5c entries parse, leaf and intermediate carry the Apple marker OIDs, the chain validates to the pinned root at the payload's own signedDate, and the payload is still valid base64url JSON naming the configured bundle id and an accepted environment. INVALID_SIGNATURE is therefore the first verdict reachable, and this is the vector that makes every port agree on the answer to "these bytes were altered" — until now each port only asserted it against bytes it mutated at run time, which no shared case could express.

The first x5c entry is base64 of the ASCII text "not a certificate" — well-formed base64 that decodes to bytes no X.509 parser can read. The header was signed in that state, so the signature genuinely covers what is served and the unparseable leaf is the only defect. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE rather than INVALID_JWS_FORMAT (the entry is present, is a string, and the array still holds exactly three) and rather than INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (nothing was parsed, so no marker OID could be looked for). The entry chosen is x5c[0] on purpose: Java parses the third entry and the other eight ports never touch it, so a vector built on x5c[2] would pin a divergence instead of a shared rule.

One byte of the receipt's signed payload was flipped after signing, so the CMS content digest no longer matches the one the signature covers. The signature segment of a genuine, verifying transaction is padded to a multiple of four with '='. The statically typed ports get this from decoding the header into an array of strings; the dynamically typed ones have to check it, and Python did not until fuzzing walked a TypeError out of base64.b64decode and past every `except` in the library. A port that reads only the entries it uses would also have to be caught by this vector, which is why all three are numbers rather than just the leaf.

The payload claims `signedDate: 1e300` — about 10^289 years, a valid JSON number that no calendar type can hold. Certificate validity is judged at the payload signing date (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4), and an instant that cannot be expressed is inside no validity window, so the verdict is INVALID_CHAIN. The ports reach it by different routes and must agree on the answer: Node builds an Invalid Date, whose every comparison is false; Python refuses to build the datetime at all and has to turn the OverflowError into this verdict rather than let it escape. NaN and Infinity land in the same place in the ports whose JSON parser accepts them, but most reject both outright, so the vector is the huge-but-valid number rather than a value half the ports cannot even parse.

One byte of x5c[1] is changed: the basicConstraints extnValue OCTET STRING is left claiming 127 content bytes inside an extension that declares 15, so the certificate stops decoding partway through its extension block. Everything before that region is intact and the header was signed in this state. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE — the entry is present, is a string and decodes from base64, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. What this vector pins that `transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate` cannot is that a port must PARSE an x5c certificate rather than scan it: the corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1" accepts the whole JWS. It is x5c[1] rather than x5c[0] so that the two certificate vectors cover both entries every port loads.

x5c[1]'s namedCurve is rewritten to 1.2.840.10045.3.1.10, which is unassigned, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so the certificate is genuine in every other respect and a broken issuer signature is not what a port objects to first. A public key cannot be built on a curve the implementation does not have, so the certificate is one this library never understood: INVALID_CERTIFICATE, alongside the other two x5c defects, rather than INVALID_CHAIN. That reading was adopted AGAINST the six-to-three majority the ports arrived with, because the three in the minority (java, swift, go) reject the certificate while decoding it and pinning INVALID_CHAIN would have required them to defer a rejection they already make. It also closes a latent escape in Node, where reading the certificate's public key raises a raw OpenSSL decode error and only the order of the issuer check kept it from reaching a caller. The requirement underneath the reason is that the failure is a verdict at all: an unimplemented curve surfaces as a library-specific exception type — cryptography's UnsupportedAlgorithm was not in Python's except list — and a caller catching the verification error sees a crash instead.

x5c[1] claims X.509 version 11, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so nothing else about it is wrong: the extensions decode, the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, and it really did issue the leaf. X.509 defines v1, v2 and v3 and nothing else, so the only thing that can reject this input is a version check, which is why a port without one accepts a certificate whose format it does not know. INVALID_CERTIFICATE: the bytes are not a certificate this library can be said to have understood, and the fault is in the certificate rather than in the path it sits on.

x5c[0] carries its basicConstraints extension twice — a byte-identical second copy appended to the extension list — and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate so the certificate is genuine in every other respect: the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, the key is the one that signed the JWS, and the intermediate really did issue it. RFC 5280 4.2 says a certificate MUST NOT include more than one instance of a particular extension, and a parser that allows one has to pick a copy, so two ports reading the same bytes can disagree about whether the certificate is a CA, what it may be used for, or whether it carries a marker OID at all. INVALID_CERTIFICATE for the same reason as transaction/reject-x5c-corrupt-extension: the entry is present, is a string, and decodes, but what comes out is not a certificate this library can be said to have read. It is not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, which would say the extensions were read and the marker OID was missing. The duplicated extension is basicConstraints rather than the marker OID because it is the one every port reaches: a port that scans for 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 and never decodes the rest of the block accepts this JWS. It sits on the leaf because that is the certificate whose extensions every port touches first, and Python's fuzzer found it there — cryptography raises DuplicateExtension, which derives from Exception rather than ValueError and so passed every except in the JWS path and reached the caller as a crash.

The signer's KEY is the mutation. One byte of the signer certificate is changed, and it is one byte further in than the JWS twin changes. transaction/reject-x5c-corrupt-extension rewrites the extnValue OCTET STRING's own length, which breaks the DER of everything that contains it — harmless in a JWS header, where the certificate is a base64 string of its own, and wrong inside a CMS, where it would break the receipt's DER and make every port that walks the whole blob answer about the receipt instead of about the certificate. So the corruption sits INSIDE the OCTET STRING: the BasicConstraints SEQUENCE it holds is left claiming 127 content bytes in a two-byte value. A reader walking generic ASN.1 sees a well-formed primitive of the length it declares and never looks in, so the receipt parses, the chain validates, the payload is intact and the CMS signature is real; only a reader that DECODES the signer's extension block finds the defect, and that is precisely what this vector observes. The certificate has no TBS left to re-sign and no verifier can reach its signature to notice. INVALID_CERTIFICATE: the signer is embedded and is the certificate the SignerInfo names, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. The corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1" accepts the whole receipt.

The SignerInfo names an issuer and serial no embedded entry carries, and the bag also holds one entry that is not a certificate. The two are separate defects and only one of them is the receipt's answer. The signing certificate is a genuine receipt-signing leaf under the genuine intermediate and it really did sign this payload; it is simply not embedded, which is INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT — the verdict every port already gives a receipt naming a signer it does not carry. The malformed stranger must not change that: it is unrelated to the SignerInfo, and blaming it would report INVALID_CERTIFICATE, which says the signer was found and was defective. The stranger is a SEQUENCE holding a TBS that stops after the issuer — no validity, no subject, no public key, no signature — so every X.509 decoder refuses it while its own version, serial and issuer stay legible. That is deliberate: a port cannot pass this by failing to read identities at all, only by reading the identity out of each entry's raw DER and comparing it to the SignerInfo before it judges any entry. Node, Swift and Go did that already; python, rust, java, php and ruby matched the SignerInfo against the entries they could DECODE and then blamed the one they could not, which is a guess whenever the signer is absent for reasons of its own.

The whole input is `..` — two dots and nothing else. It splits into exactly three segments, so a port that counts them and stops gets past that check with no header to read, and every later step is then working from nothing. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT. This is the shortest input in the vector set and the one java's fuzzing walked out of the library as a NullPointerException rather than a verdict: Jackson's readTree returns null for zero bytes, and the next line asks that null for `alg`. What the vector requires is what every negative vector requires — that the answer is a verdict a caller can catch on the error type it was told to catch.

The header segment is empty and the payload and signature are the genuine ones from a real JWS over the fixture root, so the empty header is the only defect. An empty segment is valid base64url of zero bytes, and zero bytes are not a JSON object — the distinction that matters, because a decoder that answers \"nothing\" instead of raising hands the caller a null the next line dereferences. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT, the same verdict a header that is not base64url JSON gets, and reached before any certificate is decoded.

The payload segment is empty; the header and the signature are the genuine ones, so a port reaches the payload at all rather than answering about a fake header's certificates. Zero bytes are not a JSON object, so there are no claims — and reading them as absent rather than refusing them is a fail-open: a payload stating no signedDate moves certificate validity onto the current-time fallback PLAN.md 2.1 step 4 reserves for a payload that states none, and silences the staleness rule with it. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT, decided before the signature check, which is where the payload has to be read anyway because it names the instant the chain is judged at.

The header segment is valid base64url of `[\"ES256\",[]]` — valid JSON, and not an object. RFC 7515 7.1 makes the JOSE header a JSON object; an array has no member to read `alg` or `x5c` from, and a port that indexes into it by name has to decide that on purpose rather than discover it by accident. The array's contents are chosen to look like the two things a header carries, so a port that pattern-matches rather than reads members cannot pass by luck. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT.

The header segment decodes to `42`. RFC 8259 2 makes a bare scalar a complete JSON text, so a port that asks only \"does this parse as JSON\" accepts it and then reads `alg` off a number. It is the second of the two non-object shapes a JSON document can take, and it is here beside the array because the ports' JSON readers fail differently on the two: a statically typed decode into a map refuses both, a dynamically typed one refuses neither until something checks. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT.

The payload segment decodes to `[1,2,3]` under the genuine header, so this is a verdict about the payload rather than about a fake header's certificates. Every claim a port reads by name — bundleId, environment, signedDate — is simply absent from an array, and a port that treats absent as \"not stated\" rather than refusing the payload fails open twice over: certificate validity falls back to the current time and the staleness rule stops applying, the same pair transaction/reject-signed-date-out-of-range guards from the other side. INVALID_JWS_FORMAT.

The byte half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of 1,034,681 bytes of DER, which every port MUST accept. It was sized to 98.7% of the 1,048,576 bytes the contract promised when it was written; the promise is now Apple's 3,145,728, and receipt/accept-der-at-the-size-cap holds that number exactly, so this receipt stays as the node-light, byte-heavy half of the floor pair. Its payload attribute set holds 9,237 nodes, under half the node budget, so what accepting it says is about bytes and nothing else; receipt/verify-at-the-node-floor pins the other number the same way round. Two receipts rather than one because a single fixture under both limits lets a port lower either cap to just above what that one fixture happens to use — the receipt this pair replaces was 809,069 bytes and 16,037 nodes, and a port capping at 900,000 bytes or 17,000 nodes passed it. The size is 2,300 in-app purchases and nothing else: no padding attribute and no inflated wrapper, only product ids padded to 262 characters, which sit in the value of a MODELLED attribute a port must decode and return. The fields pin the collection so a port cannot pass by truncating it, and the first and last purchases keep short product ids so a case can select them by one. endpoint/verify-at-the-byte-floor runs the same receipt through the endpoint.

The node half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt whose payload attribute set is one parse of 19,897 nodes — 99.5% of the 20,000 the contract promises — which every port MUST accept. It is 74,569 bytes, a fourteenth of the byte floor, so what accepting it says is about the node budget alone. Ten in-app purchases carry the receipt's real shape; the node count comes from 4,955 further attributes of three bytes each whose types this library does not model. That is the honest shape for this number rather than a shortcut: a node budget is spent per TLV walked, whatever the TLV means, and an unmodelled attribute is walked, counted and recorded under unknownAttributes like any other — the fields below pin two of them, at each end of the run, so a port cannot pass by skipping what it does not recognise. Building the same node count out of in-app purchases would have cost a megabyte of repository for a fixture whose whole subject is the count.

Four legacy attributes every port used to leave raw in unknownAttributes are decoded instead: app-level 1 (app item id), 15 (download id) and 16 (version external identifier), and in-app 1713 (is trial period). None of the four is on Apple's archived Receipt Fields chapter; they were established by decoding a genuine production receipt and lining its attributes up against the answer Apple's verifyReceipt endpoint gives for the same receipt (measured 2026-09-21). All four are INTEGER attributes and decode like 1711. The download id is 2^53+1, the first integer an IEEE-754 double cannot hold: Apple's real download_id values run to eighteen digits, so a port must carry these exactly rather than as a JavaScript number, and one that rounds answers 9007199254740992 here. The two purchases carry 1713 on both sides of the boolean, so no port passes by rendering one constant.

A receipt carrying none of the four attributes reports them absent rather than zero or empty: the shared sandbox receipt has no 1, 15, 16 or 1713, so appItemId, downloadId, versionExternalIdentifier and a purchase's isTrialPeriod are all null. Absent and present-but-zero are different answers, and the value 0 is what Apple's sandbox sends for the three ids when it does carry them.

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint echoes the four decoded attributes under Apple's own keys and in Apple's own JSON types. Attribute 1 appears TWICE, as adam_id and as app_item_id, because Apple's response reference defines adam_id as "See app_item_id" and both carry the same value. The three app-level ids are JSON numbers, unlike the in-app integers, which Apple renders as strings; download_id is 2^53+1, so a port serialising through a double answers 9007199254740992 and fails. Attribute 1713 becomes is_trial_period, the string "true" or "false", exactly as 1719 becomes is_in_intro_offer_period. This case pins no clock, so request_date* is left unasserted.

An attribute the receipt does not carry leaves its key OUT of the endpoint's answer rather than emitting JSON null: the shared sandbox receipt carries none of the four, so adam_id, app_item_id, download_id, version_external_identifier and a purchase's is_trial_period are all absent. That is what Apple does, and it is what the existing optional keys already do here.

A genuine sandbox receipt carries attribute types 1, 15 and 16 with value 0, and 1713 with value 0 on every in-app entry, which is what Apple's verifyReceipt echoes as adam_id, app_item_id, download_id, version_external_identifier and is_trial_period for a sandbox receipt. Present-with-zero is a decoded 0, not absent: receipt/ids-absent-when-not-carried pins the other case.

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint renders the zero-valued ids a genuine sandbox receipt carries exactly as Apple does for a sandbox receipt: adam_id, app_item_id, download_id and version_external_identifier as the JSON number 0, and is_trial_period as the string "false".

The device-hash rule is pinned against Apple-signed bytes, not only against a receipt this repository generated: tikhop/TPInAppReceipt's HashVerifierTests publishes the device identifier of the genuine sandbox receipt vendored here, and SHA1(deviceId bytes || attribute 4 || the DER of attribute 2) over it reproduces attribute 5 byte for byte. A port whose concatenation order, UUID byte order or bundle-id encoding is wrong cannot pass this one by agreeing with the generator that produced the fixture.

The same Apple-signed receipt under a device identifier that differs in its first byte only is rejected on the device hash. The positive twin is what makes this one mean something: a port that never computes the hash would pass one of the pair and fail the other.

Attribute 2 is compared byte for byte, not case-insensitively: a configured bundle id that differs from the receipt's only in the case of one letter is a different app. Bundle ids are case-sensitive to Apple, and a port that folds case here would accept a receipt issued for a bundle id its caller does not own. receipt/reject-wrong-bundle-id pins a wholly different id; this pins the near miss.

The certificate sitting where the intermediate belongs is a receipt-signing end entity, and the signer really was issued by it. Every signature and every name link in the path is genuine, every validity window covers the receipt's creation date, and the path terminates at the pinned root; the only defect is that basicConstraints says that certificate may not issue. A port that chains on issuer names and signatures alone accepts it, which would let any receipt-signing leaf mint signers of its own.

A genuine signer under a genuine intermediate, with the intermediate left out of the CMS certificate bag, so no path reaches the pinned root. Paired with receipt/reject-leaf-presented-as-intermediate it separates the two ways an issuer can be wrong: absent, and present but not a CA.

The SignerInfo's signature is an OCTET STRING of zero bytes. DER length-prefixes it, so an empty signature is well-formed ASN.1 and the receipt parses, the chain builds and the signer purpose checks out: the port has to reach the verification step and take a negative answer from it. A port that treats an empty signature as a parse failure, or that skips verification when there is nothing to verify, answers something else.

A CMS whose encapsulated content is zero bytes long. It is signed over those zero bytes rather than emptied afterwards, so the chain, the signer purpose and the signature are all genuine. Content that is present but empty passes the CMS parse; the step-2 walk finds no attribute SET, so the chain is judged at the system clock; and the full payload parse then has nothing to read. A trusted signer signed content the library cannot read: INTERNAL_ERROR. Attribute 2 can never be read from it, so accepting it would mean accepting a receipt that states no bundle id at all. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

Attribute 12 is present and reads "not-a-date". Step 2 cannot use it, and an unreadable date cannot blame anyone before trust is established, so it only moves the chain instant to the system clock. The chain is valid then, the signer carries the receipt-signing OID and the signature verifies; the full payload parse then refuses the same date. A trusted signer signed content the library cannot read: INTERNAL_ERROR, never INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

The same unreadable creation date, signed by a PKI with the same subject names that the verifier does not trust. The chain is built before anything but the creation date is read, so the answer is INVALID_CHAIN: an unreadable payload from an untrusted signer must not surface as a format error, and must never reach INTERNAL_ERROR, which only a trusted signer can earn. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

The unreadable creation date under a trusted chain that has expired. Judged at the system clock the chain is out of its window, so INVALID_CHAIN. This is what shows the fallback instant really is "now" rather than no validity check at all: a port that skipped the window when the date was unusable would go on to answer INTERNAL_ERROR. The chain was valid only from 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01, so judged at the system clock it has expired on every run, while every date the payload states lies inside that window.

A readable creation date inside the chain's window, a trusted chain and a valid signature; one in-app purchase (attribute 17) whose value is an OCTET STRING rather than an attribute SET. Step 2 reads only attribute 12 and never decodes attribute 17, so everything up to the signature passes, and the full parse is the first place the in-app purchase is looked at. INTERNAL_ERROR: the fault is in content a trusted signer signed, not in the client's request. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

Attribute 12 appears twice, both times with a date inside the chain's window. Two creation dates are no usable creation date, so the chain is judged at the system clock and has expired: INVALID_CHAIN. A port that took the first or the last of the two would accept. The chain was valid only from 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01, so judged at the system clock it has expired on every run, while every date the payload states lies inside that window.

A readable creation date inside the chain's window beside one top-level entry that is SEQUENCE { INTEGER } instead of SEQUENCE { INTEGER, INTEGER, OCTET STRING }. An entry the step-2 walk cannot read fails the walk as a whole, since that entry might have been a second attribute 12; the readable date is not used and the chain is judged at the system clock: INVALID_CHAIN. The chain was valid only from 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01, so judged at the system clock it has expired on every run, while every date the payload states lies inside that window.

The same unreadable top-level entry beside a readable creation date, under a trusted chain valid at the system clock. The walk fails, the chain is judged at now and passes, the signature verifies, and the full parse refuses the entry: INTERNAL_ERROR. The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

The unreadable-creation-date receipt at the endpoint. It authenticates, so it is not 21003, and the client did nothing wrong, so it is not 21002: status 21009 with INTERNAL_ERROR, the status an integrator must treat as "alert and retry, do not deny the user". The test PKI is valid from 2024-01-01 to 2050-01-01, so judging it at the system clock gives the same answer on every run until 2050.

A genuinely signed receipt of exactly 2,359,296 bytes of DER, whose canonical base64 is exactly 3,145,728 characters: the receipt cap, which is Apple's own request limit. receipt-data must be canonical base64 with nothing around it, so this is the only way a string at the cap can still verify. It is the byte-floor shape, the same 2,300 in-app purchases, with the padded product ids lengthened to 836 characters and one of them further by whatever the total still needed, written by java/src/test/.../ReceiptBase64CapFixture.java under a root of its own. A port whose cap sits below 3 MiB, or that measures the decoded length instead of the string it was handed, answers INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT. The fields pin the collection so a port cannot pass by truncating it.

The at-cap string of receipt-base64/accept-at-the-size-cap with one line feed appended: 3,145,729 bytes, one over the receipt cap, refused as INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT before it is decoded. Since receipt-data became canonical base64 only, no string over the cap could verify without the cap either (its length is not a multiple of four, and the line feed is refused on its own), so the verdict here is the same whichever check fires first; each port's own input-cap test pins that the length is checked before the decode.

No padding: four data characters, three bytes. Apple's verifyReceipt accepted this shape of genuine receipts, production and sandbox, on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md), so both decoders do.

One '=': the canonical 'QUI=' and the three spellings whose last data character has its two unused low bits set. Apple's verifyReceipt accepted this shape of genuine receipts, production and sandbox, on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md), so both decoders do. The rule checks the alphabet, the padding and the length, never the trailing bits, so a decoder that refuses them (Go's StdEncoding.Strict(), Ruby's strict_decode64, the base64 crate's default engine, System.Buffers.Text.Base64) answers INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT where Apple answers 0.

Two '=': the canonical 'QQ==' and all fifteen spellings whose last data character has some of its four unused low bits set, 'QR==' through 'Qf=='. Apple's verifyReceipt accepted this shape of genuine receipts, production and sandbox, on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md), so both decoders do. Every value of the unused bits is listed, so a decoder that masks the wrong bits cannot pass on a lucky subset.

The two characters outside the letters and digits, '+' and '/', each in a data position and as the last data character with its unused bits set. A decoder whose table maps them wrongly, or maps base64url's '-' and '_' onto the same values, is caught here and in base64/reject-base64url.
Two groups, the second padded with '=='; 'AQIDBP==' sets all four unused bits of the last data character. The canonical spelling is the tiny receipt the endpoint suites send.

Three full groups and no padding: the base the junk, whitespace and base64url insertions of the x5c tests are spliced into (base64/reject-junk-inside, base64/reject-whitespace-inside, base64/reject-base64url).
Seven bytes, two groups and '=='; the second spelling sets the last character's unused bits. Its unpadded form, 'QUJDREVGRw', is in base64/reject-padding-omitted.

All 64 characters of the standard alphabet in order, which is canonical base64 of 48 bytes. A hand-written table with one wrong entry, or a range check off by one at any of 'A', 'Z', 'a', 'z', '0', '9', '+' and '/', decodes this to other bytes.
Eighty characters on one line, the unwrapped form of the base64/reject-line-breaks spellings: one line is the only way long base64 is accepted.

Canonical base64 of bytes that are not DER. The base64 is valid, so both decoders return the bytes; refusing them is the certificate or CMS parser's job, which the rust suite's x5c tests and the verifyTransaction vectors pin, and which is a different stage from the one this operation pins.
Canonical base64 with no padding of bytes that are not DER, the x5c[2] entry of the rust suite's third-entry test. Valid base64, so both decoders return the bytes.

The shared generated receipt followed by zero bytes, 3,145,729 bytes of DER in all: one over the receipt cap. DER has no padding, so no oversized input can verify without the cap; this one would be refused for its trailing bytes anyway, with the same reason. What it pins is that the cap is 3 MiB of DER, that the refusal is a verdict rather than a crash or an allocation failure, and that it is INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT. receipt/accept-der-at-the-size-cap holds the accepting side with a genuinely signed receipt of exactly 3,145,728 bytes, and receipt/reject-signed-der-one-byte-over-the-size-cap is its well-formed twin one byte longer, which only the cap can refuse.

The accepting side of the DER cap: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of exactly 3,145,728 bytes, which every port MUST accept. It is the byte-floor shape grown to the cap: the same 2,300 in-app purchases, no padding attribute and no inflated wrapper, with the padded product ids lengthened to 1,176 characters and one of them further by whatever the total still needed. Its payload attribute set holds 9,237 nodes, so a node budget cannot be what decides it; a port that refuses it is refusing bytes it promised to take. Only the raw-DER entry point can carry it: the base64 cap is 3,145,728 characters, which decode to at most 2,359,296 bytes, so neither verifyReceiptBase64 nor the endpoint can reach a DER receipt this large. The fields pin the collection so a port cannot pass by truncating it.

The twin of receipt/accept-der-at-the-size-cap, one product-id character longer: 3,145,729 bytes of DER that are well-formed and correctly signed under the same root, with nothing after the structure. receipt/reject-der-one-byte-over-the-size-cap is refused for trailing bytes too, so a port could pass it without any cap at all; this receipt is genuine in every respect but its length, so only the 3,145,728-byte cap can refuse it, as INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT.

A verifying request body, {"receipt-data":"<the genuine sandbox receipt>"}, padded with JSON whitespace before its closing brace to exactly 3,145,728 bytes. Apple answers a body of this size normally (measured 2026-09-23 on production and sandbox), so the endpoint must too: status 0.

The same body with one more space: 3,145,729 bytes. Apple answers HTTP 413 at exactly this size, so the endpoint answers status 21002 with the result-only reason REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, which a caller's HTTP layer maps to 413. The body is refused before it is parsed; without the cap it verifies.

A verifying request body whose password field (accepted for wire compatibility and never read) holds U+00E9, a two-byte character, filling the body to exactly 3,145,728 UTF-8 bytes in 1,576,659 characters. The cap counts bytes, so this is at the cap, not over it: status 0. A port that overestimates, for example by charging three bytes for every character, refuses it.

The same shape at 3,145,729 UTF-8 bytes, which is only 1,576,659 characters. Apple counts bytes: 3,145,729 bytes of U+00E9 (1,572,874 characters) got HTTP 413 on 2026-09-23. So this is 21002 with REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, and a port that measures the body in characters (UTF-16 code units or code points) answers 0 instead.
A verifying request body carrying an ignored field of 63 nested arrays, so the body object and the arrays are 64 containers open at once: exactly the nesting limit. It verifies, status 0.

The same body with one more array, 65 containers deep: one past the nesting limit. 21002 with MALFORMED_REQUEST, not REQUEST_TOO_LARGE: the body is small, and depth is a shape the envelope may not have. Without the limit it verifies.

The 3,145,729-byte receipt string of receipt-base64/reject-one-byte-over-the-size-cap as receipt-data, handed to the endpoint's structured entry point (the one that takes an already-parsed request, so no body cap applies). The receipt cap answers, so the reason stays INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT, not REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, and the status is 21002. A harness that can only reach a JSON-body entry point wraps this in a body over the request cap and so cannot check the reason; it still gets 21002.

The 1,034,681-byte receipt of receipt/verify-at-the-byte-floor through the endpoint: its base64 is 1,379,576 characters, well inside the 3 MiB request cap, so it answers 0 with every purchase rendered.

Apple's mock renewal-info JWS with its signature segment extended by base64url 'A' characters to exactly 262,144 bytes, the JWS cap. At the cap nothing is refused for size, so a port decodes the header and certificates, builds the chain and reaches the signature, which is now far longer than the 64 bytes ES256 takes: INVALID_SIGNATURE. A port whose cap sits lower answers INVALID_JWS_FORMAT. The segment length avoids 1 mod 4 and 'A' carries no stray bits, so the segment is canonical base64url.
The same JWS one 'A' longer: 262,145 bytes, one over the cap. Refused before it is split or decoded, as INVALID_JWS_FORMAT; without the cap it would be INVALID_SIGNATURE like its neighbour.

A raw request body whose receipt-data is the genuine sandbox receipt's canonical base64 (01-genuine) with U+FEFF in front of it, the mark written as its UTF-8 bytes rather than as a JSON escape. Apple's verifyReceipt answered 21002 to a byte-order mark before the string on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md, "Around the string"): U+FEFF is outside the base64 alphabet, so this is INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT like any other character there. What makes it worth a case of its own is the JSON parser, not the base64 rule: Foundation's JSONSerialization drops a leading U+FEFF from a string value (always on Darwin, where strings are built through NSString), so a port that parses the body with it hands the decoder the genuine base64 and answers 0. The input is the whole body, so the port's own parser is what reads it.

The shared generated receipt, genuine and correctly signed, followed by one zero byte. Every port refuses bytes after the receipt's DER (THREAT-MODEL.md section 3.7), and this case pins that in the shared suite: INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT. Apple's verifyReceipt does NOT refuse this shape: on 2026-09-23 it decoded genuine receipts followed by one zero byte and by several other tails, reading the first complete value and ignoring the rest (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md, "Bytes after the receipt"). The library is deliberately stricter here, the one place it is: no genuine client produces trailing bytes, since appStoreReceiptURL yields the exact file, and refusing them keeps one receipt to one byte string.

The endpoint twin of receipt/reject-one-trailing-byte-after-the-der: the same DER, a genuine receipt followed by one zero byte, canonically base64-encoded into receipt-data. 21002 with INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT. Apple's endpoint decodes a genuine receipt with bytes after it and answers as if they were absent, so this is a deliberate divergence from Apple, for the reason that case gives.
